newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Lithuania set for vote, Landsbergis eyes power.
newsitem.headline: Lithuania set for vote, Landsbergis eyes power.

text.p: The Baltic state of Lithuania was preparing for elections on Saturday in which independence hero Vytautas Landsbergis is bidding to unseat his bitter foes from the ruling former Communist party.
Voting starts on Sunday for a parliament where chunks of grafitti-covered concrete barricades still stand as a striking reminder of the country's fight to quit the former Soviet Union.

Landsbergis, a former music teacher, put Lithuania's independence movement on the map in January 1991. Thirteen people died when Soviet troops seized the television tower in Vilnius, a centre of the anti-Soviet movement.

But as the country's economy collapsed in the wake of independence, people turned against Landsbergis in 1992 elections in favour of the familiar: the reform Communists of the Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP).
The LDLP sealed its victory the following year as leader Algirdas Brazauskas won presidential elections.
Their victory started a trend in eastern Europe where a population hit by economic crisis and soaring inflation propelled former Communists back into power.
A campaign blackout was in force on Saturday ahead of Sunday's vote. A second-round run-off is set for November 10.
In the second election since the country regained its independence in 1991, people will choose from 1,351 candidates and 24 parties. They also have to vote in four referenda.
Opinion polls suggest Landsbergis' Homeland Union party has a good chance of being the largest party in parliament although analysts say his comeback will not be straightforward.
"We are going to have a coalition, that is for sure," Lars Johanssen, a political scientist from Denmark's Aarhus University and an expert on Lithuanian politics, told Reuters.
After four years in power, the LDLP have been accused of reneging on their populist promises to ease the pain of reform and have been discredited by accusations of corruption.
Although it made macroeconomic gains and cut inflation, many people, especially pensioners and unemployed, live on a pittance and have failed to see the benefits of a market economy.
Their rating reached a low during a bank crisis at the end of last year when a former prime minister withdrew his personal savings from a bank days before it was shut.
Landsbergis's party will ally with the Christian Democrats, who stress "traditional values" in this strongly Roman Catholic country, as the core of a right-of-centre coalition.
But Lithuanians have shown little enthusiasm for the election and there are a large number of undecided people.
Analysts say there is room for surprise and a possible protest vote amid general cynicism.
"Some Lithuanians seek a third force," said Arturas Racas, political writer on leading daily Lietuvos rytas.
He said some people were tired of the fight between Landsbergis and the LDLP and already knew them as rulers.
Racas said a search for a third force may favour the populist Centre Union party or more radically the far-right Young Lithuanians, who have promised to be tough on crime.
